An absolute masterclass in anti-consumer user interface design that turns simply launching a video game into an infuriating chore.

Originally introduced as Activision's vision for a unified, "one-stop shop" hub for the entire franchise, the Call of Duty HQ launcher stands as one of the most hated executable files on Steam. Rather than streamlining access to your purchased games, it acts as a massive, bloated barrier. Booting up a game requires opening the HQ launcher first, staring at a cluttered screen covered in seasonal battle pass advertisements and microtransaction store banners, and selecting your game mode—only for the launcher to completely shut itself down and force your PC to boot up another separate executable just to play Warzone or an older campaign. It is an uninspired, clunky time-sink that treats your gaming library like a glorified, interactive billboard.

The technical headaches caused by this ecosystem are legendary. Because the HQ forces multiple games to share overlapping code and asset files, routine title updates constantly result in file corruption, wiped graphic settings, or massive 80GB-plus downloads just to patch a hotfix for a game mode you might not even play. To make matters worse, the launcher frequently locks up, demanding a complete game restart for every minor playlist update or shader optimization pass. It creates a ridiculous double-boot cycle where you spend five to ten minutes just fighting through application restarts, menu reloads, and crashing launchers before you can step foot onto a multiplayer map.

Ultimately, the ecosystem felt less like a feature built for player convenience and more like a corporate scheme to artificially pad player "engagement time" and push storefront sales. The community pushback grew so toxic that developers eventually had to start uncoupling games from the bloated hub to let players launch them as standalone titles again. claims.claim: Reviewers describe encountering cheaters and hackers in online matches despite anti-cheat systems.

citations.review_text:
It’s a good game, but it constantly pushes out massive updates,
and there are quite a few cheaters, so I wouldn't recommend it.

[h1]Questionable Engagement Tactics[/h1]

Call of Duty has shifted from being a premium shooter to a product built around continuous behavioral pressure. The modern structure feels less like a game purchase and more like a recurring subscription disguised as seasonal content. The base price is already high, but the battle pass and rotating cosmetic bundles create a spending cycle that encourages players to stay financially committed. Progression systems, time limited rewards, and constant resets are designed to keep players engaged through psychological pressure rather than genuine gameplay depth.

Despite repeated claims of improved safeguards, [b][u]cheating remains rampant[/u][/b]. The developer frequently promotes new detection methods and anti cheat technology, yet the in game experience shows that cheaters are still widespread and highly visible. The gap between marketing and reality raises serious questions about whether these systems are effective or simply meant to reassure paying customers.

Enforcement is equally concerning. Automated bans, limited transparency, and minimal customer support leave players vulnerable to losing access to a product they have invested significant money into. The appeal process is unclear, slow, or nonexistent, and the platform often treats legitimate players the same as actual offenders.

[h2]Key Concerns[/h2]
[b]• Monetization pressure[/b]
The cost structure resembles a subscription more than a one time purchase.
[b]• Psychological engagement tactics[/b]
Progress bars, time limited items, and seasonal resets encourage compulsive play.
[b]• [u]Rampant cheating[/u][/b]
Cheaters remain common despite repeated claims of improved safeguards.
[b]• Opaque enforcement systems[/b]
Automated bans and limited support create risk for legitimate players.
[b]• Seasonal resets[/b]
Progress loses relevance every season, pushing players toward new purchases.

I used to like this game a lot. Then came the hordes of cheaters... then came the 300 gb of space it requires to play almost any part of this game. I played MW, MW2, Black Op 1/2/3, ect... Call of duty is not the same and neither is the community. I liked it because it was a shooter that had realistic guns and fun maps... Now, you get shot by laser bullets by people in furry costumes.... ect. Is some of it still fun? yes. Is it worth the weekly updates, the 300gb of storage, and putting up with being in a 30 minute match just to get snap shot by every bullet from an SMG across the map/sniper shot through walls/shot through the floor of the map while in the top 10? I think not. 

P.S. I have wayyyy more hours on Blizzard launcher. This is not just some cranky old man (30s) whining about the changing of times. I really feels like COD doesn't care about its identity or its customers so long as it gets its $$$.
game is terrible they banned my xbox acc for being AFK while cheaters run wild and free!

incompatible with windows. every other update destroys a file so you have to manually delete and reinstall, or mess with cmd and file permissions due to the anti cheat that litteraly doesnt even stop cheaters

Everyone is having very negative reviews... This is the first "new COD" I have gotten and really enjoyed.  (I did technically play some Cold War and love that for Outbreak and local console coop). Moving from bo2, to IW, to bo3... I like the movement a lot.  The GUI is extremely overwhelming at first, but it's really so incredibly easy to ignore it, just worry about loadouts, and search for a lobby.  Multiplayer is solid, and although the matchmaking is clearly SBMM, I haven't had a bad time at all, and it has been extremely enjoyable.  I was only in one lobby of hackers, but all they had was their level pinned at level 1, and I assume it was some sort of profile boost.  (After 5 games with them, none of them had leveled up even though they were getting instakills; one player had wallhacks or something, but even those games were enjoyable.  Zombies is a WHOLE NEW BEAST compared to BO3.  In some ways, it is easier; in many others, it is just as hard, or harder.  It's really weird, but this year's zombie maps have been great (we didn't need another Nuketown, but whatever...).  As far as performance, I was very happy to find that my "old" laptop from 2021 handles the game excellently. My computer well exceeds the minimum requirements, not the recommended, but I'm playing at a stable locked 60fps as limited by my cheap monitor.  I'm a casual gamer, but the double XP weekend really let me crunch through prestige 1 easy peasy.  Overall, I'm really enjoying the game... My worst issue is that it is entirely online, so if the game player base dies off, I doubt I can even play solo zombies.  I ALWAYS wait for sales, so I don't have any issue paying for it with the quality of Kowakujo.  Also, the freaking download size is ungodly at over 200GB... I was expecting something around 100, but double that is insane.  I had plenty of space, but holy crap.  If you are a bum and angry at CODs in general, you will hate the game, but I loved IW from launch and TranZit with my buddies on …

Littered with bugs, rushed content, and shallow nostalgia bait. But at least you can spend $30 on a SINGLE operator and weapon skin. This game series is a great example of how corporate greed has destroyed AAA gaming.

I do not hate Call of Duty. In fact, I have loved a lot of these games over the years, and the story modes across the franchise have had some amazing moments. My issue is not with the idea of Call of Duty itself. My issue is with what the franchise and the company behind it have become.

I have spent thousands of dollars on Call of Duty over the years, probably somewhere around $8,000–$10,000 across games, bundles, battle passes, COD Points, and other content. At this point, it feels less like a game series I own and more like an ecosystem I am only temporarily allowed to access.

The launcher/multiplayer hub has also been a mess. Yes, some issues have been fixed over time, but fixing one broken launch system does not erase the bigger problems. Even accessing content I already paid for can feel like jumping through hoops.

The biggest issue for me is the ownership problem. You do not really own your copy. You do not own the COD Points you just bought. You do not own the bundles, skins, or digital content in the way most normal people understand ownership. You are basically renting access until they decide the movie has expired.

Now, with the new EULA, continued access to previously purchased digital goods and multiplayer services is being conditioned on broad, high-privilege device-monitoring consent without clear, enforceable, auditable limits. Companies sell digital games using words like “buy” and “purchase,” but then legally define them as temporary licensed access. They condition continued use on terms normal players cannot negotiate, cannot meaningfully verify, and often cannot refuse without losing access to things they already paid for. That should not be legal or be normal.

The matchmaking experience has also become extremely frustrating. One match can feel smooth and fair, where my shots register and I leave with a 2.7–3.2 K/D. The very next match can feel completely different: lag, desync, dying behind cover, shots not registering, and players appearing…
